rows.value: W. Rhoads Murphey was a geographer and historian of Asia, specializing in the modern history and geography of China and South Asia. Educated at Harvard University under John K. Fairbank, he earned his Ph.D. in Far Eastern history and geography in 1950 and taught at the University of Washington and University of Michigan. Murphey “wrote or co-authored a dozen books,” focusing on “the modern history of urbanization in the region” as in Shanghai: Key to Modern China (1953), and gained recognition with The Outsiders: Westerners in India and China (1977), which won an award for best book of the year from the University of Michigan Press. His textbooks such as A History of Asia went through many editions, highlighting his role as a key educator in Asian studies. Murphey’s intellectual trajectory combined his firsthand experience during WWII serving with the British Friends Ambulance Unit in China, where he met prominent figures including Zhou Enlai and Mao Zedong, with a scholarly career that emphasized “approaches to modern Chinese history” and the interactions between East and West. He served as executive director and president of the Association for Asian Studies and edited the Journal of Asian Studies, reflecting his leadership in the field. His work is characterized by a broad geographical and historical scope, integrating political, social, and urban dimensions of Asian history. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhoads_Murphey)

rows.value: Thomas C. Smith was a distinguished historian specializing in early modern and modern Japan, whose research profoundly reshaped understandings of Japanese economic development and social change. His major works include Political Change and Industrial Development: Government Enterprise, 1868-1880 (1955), The Agrarian Origins of Modern Japan (1959), Nakahara: Family Farming and Population in a Japanese Village, 1717-1830 (1977), and Native Sources of Japanese Industrialization, 1750-1920 (1988). As Kenneth B. Pyle notes, Smith “changed our understanding of the trajectory of Japanese economic development” by arguing that “the gradual evolution of the Tokugawa agrarian economy (1600-1868), the change in the village from subsistence production to production for the market, and the transformation of family farming” played a major role in Japan’s modernization, challenging established views. Smith’s work was marked by his “amazingly wide range of methodologies” and a combination of “quantitative, highly statistical analysis with a warm eye for ordinary people,” according to colleagues, and his historiography often adopted a comparative approach that questioned the assumed universality of Western industrialization. His career path included wartime service as a Japanese language officer, followed by graduate studies culminating in a PhD from Harvard, teaching appointments at Stanford and UC Berkeley, where he was Ford Professor of History. His scholarly style was “economy, diamond-cutting words in otherwise quiet sentences, and a magisterial union of evidence and argument,” making his contributions “unrivalled” and “as close to immortal as scholarship gets,” according to Mary Elizabeth Berry. (https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/_files/inmemoriam/html/thomascsmith.htm)

Metzger, “a senior fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution,” is a leading scholar in the intellectual and institutional history of China, spanning both premodern and modern periods. His research “focuses on contemporary China's moral-political discourse and its historical roots,” and he has written extensively on U.S.–China policy. His major works include The Internal Organization of Ch'ing Bureaucracy (1973), Escape from Predicament: Neo-Confucianism and China's Evolving Political Culture (1977), and A Cloud Across the Pacific: Essays on the Clash between Chinese and Western Political Theories Today (2005). Metzger has published numerous influential articles such as “The Western Concept of the Civil Society in the Context of Chinese History” and “Continuities between Modern and Premodern China,” and his scholarship appears in both Western and Chinese academic journals. Having taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the University of California, San Diego (1970–1990), he later held distinguished appointments at institutions across Taiwan, Hong Kong, and mainland China. Recognized for his “unstinting commitment” to cross-cultural intellectual exchange, Metzger continues to be a pivotal figure in comparative political theory and Chinese intellectual history. rows.value: Roderick MacFarquhar was a British sinologist, politician, and journalist specializing in modern Chinese history, particularly Maoist China, known for his extensive scholarly works such as the three-volume The Origins of the Cultural Revolution and Mao’s Last Revolution (2006). According to Wikipedia, he was "founding editor of China Quarterly in 1959," served as a Member of Parliament in the 1970s, and later became a professor at Harvard University, where he directed the Fairbank Center for Chinese Studies. His intellectual trajectory included studies at Keble College, Oxford (BA in Philosophy, Politics and Economics), a master’s at Harvard under John King Fairbank, and completing his doctorate at the London School of Economics in 1981. His academic and journalistic career spanned roles at The Daily Telegraph, BBC’s Panorama, Columbia University, and SOAS, with a focus on "Chinese politics from the founding of the People's Republic through to the Cultural Revolution." His Origins of the Cultural Revolution series, especially volume three titled The Coming of the Cataclysm 1961-1966 (1997), won the Joseph Levenson Book Prize for 1999, underscoring his status as "a scholar of Chinese politics." His research was deeply historical and political, examining the complexities of Maoist governance and ideological shifts, and he continued to publish influential works on China’s political evolution through the late 20th century. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roderick_MacFarquhar)

rows.value: R. David Arkush was a historian specializing in modern China who served at the University of Iowa from 1974 until his retirement in 2010. According to the source, Arkush “was instrumental in building the undergraduate and graduate programs in Chinese and East Asian history,” with a scholarly focus on “China’s people and culture in an age of revolution.” His major works include Fei Xiaotong and Sociology in Revolutionary China (Harvard University Press, 1981), which “analyzed the intellectual encounter of China’s first western-trained sociologist with the profound social conflicts and ruptures in rural China,” and Land without Ghosts: Chinese impressions of America from the mid-19th century to present (University of California Press, 1989), which “unpacked the cultural constructs of Chinese visitors and their American hosts” that shaped mutual perceptions. Around 1990, his research took a “cultural studies turn” as he conducted fieldwork in rural northern China, collecting folk tales, interviewing village Chinese opera actors, and recording performances, though much of this work remained unpublished due to illness. His intellectual trajectory combined deep historical analysis with ethnographic fieldwork, emphasizing both social conflict and cultural exchange. His materials have been donated for continued scholarly use, reflecting his legacy of intellectual generosity. (https://history.uiowa.edu/people/david-arkush)

rows.value: Philip West was a “lifelong learner, teacher and scholar” whose work focused on modern East Asian history, particularly Chinese-Western and Japanese-Western relations. After earning a degree in Peace Studies from Manchester College in 1960 and serving as a conscientious objector teaching English in Poland, he pursued graduate studies at Harvard, where he studied Chinese and earned a Ph.D. in modern Chinese history and East Asian Languages in 1971. His first book, published by Harvard and focused on Yenching University and Chinese-Western relations, “was nominated for a Pulitzer award in history.” West also “wrote extensively on Japanese narratives of war” and edited two volumes on “history and war memory—one about Korea, and the other about Vietnam.” Committed to education and public understanding, he “worked to broaden and enrich the East Asian curriculum in university classrooms and public schools,” directed the East Asian Studies Center at Indiana University Bloomington for six years, and later served as director of the Maureen and Mike Mansfield Center at the University of Montana for a decade. From his early experience as a Seagoing Cowboy aiding postwar Japan to his scholarship and institutional leadership, West’s intellectual trajectory was defined by a deep commitment to peace, cross-cultural understanding, and historical memory. rows.value: Philip Kuhn was a “historian’s historian” whose research reshaped the field of modern Chinese history through “artful, deeply researched storytelling” grounded in Chinese sources and focused on internal developments rather than Western impact. His intellectual trajectory began with Chinese language training in the U.S. Army, graduate studies under John Fairbank and Benjamin Schwartz, and early teaching at the University of Chicago before joining Harvard in 1978. His first book, Rebellion and Its Enemies in Late Imperial China, challenged prevailing narratives by showing that “militarization and fragmentation… had more to do with domestic forces than with pressures from abroad.” His most popular work, Soulstealers, based on Qing archival documents, examined “a court panic born of news of sorcerers” and exposed “imperial overreach and insecurity” as well as the “empowerment of ordinary people” as an “unmet promise.” His later works, The Origins of the Modern Chinese State and Chinese Among Others: Emigration in Modern Times, further expanded his scope, with the latter placing “the history of the Chinese in a truly global context.” Revered for his rigorous seminars, Kuhn taught that “there are lies, there are damn lies, and then there are documents,” and emphasized that teaching was “our bread and butter.” Through scholarship, mentorship, and institution-building, Kuhn made enduring contributions to the study of China and the broader practice of history. (https://fairbank.fas.harvard.edu/person/philip-a-kuhn/)

He has taught courses on East Asian history and civilization, Chinese social and economic history, the Silk Road, and historical methodology. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His first book, Exhausting the Earth: State and Peasant in Hunan, 1500-1850 A.D. rows.value: Paul A. Cohen is a historian specializing in Chinese history from the nineteenth century to the present, having taught at Wellesley College for 35 years and been affiliated with the Fairbank Center since 1965. His scholarship emphasizes the interplay between history and popular memory, as exemplified in his book History and Popular Memory: The Power of Story in Moments of Crisis (2014), where he explores crises across multiple countries and reflects, “I made two discoveries: first, a book that doesn’t focus mainly on China takes a lot less time to write, and, second, there was a whole world out there that I knew next to nothing about. It was like going to college again in my retirement.” His early major works include China and Christianity: The Missionary Movement and the Growth of Chinese Antiforeignism, 1860-1870 (1963) and Between Tradition and Modernity: Wang T’ao and Reform in Late Ch’ing China (1974), which focus on reform and cultural encounters in late imperial China. He also edited and coedited significant collections such as Reform in Nineteenth-Century China (1976) and Ideas Across Cultures (1990). His influential History in Three Keys: The Boxers as Event, Experience, and Myth (1997) exemplifies his method of viewing historical events through multiple perspectives. Cohen’s intellectual trajectory moves from detailed historical studies of Chinese reform and anti-foreign movements to broader thematic analyses of history’s role in shaping collective memory and cultural narratives across nations. (https://fairbank.fas.harvard.edu/person/paul-a-cohen/)

rows.value: Mary Rankin, a student of John King Fairbank and a pivotal figure in the field of Chinese history, focused her research on late imperial and modern China, with a strong emphasis on revolutionary movements, elite activism, and local power structures. Her first book, Early Chinese Revolutionaries: Radical Intellectuals in Shanghai and Chekiang, 1902–1911 (Harvard 1971), “essentially transformed our understanding of China’s Republican Revolution of 1911” by shifting attention away from Sun Yat-sen to “groups of young people, mostly students... quite outside of Sun’s orbit,” thereby revealing the revolution as “a far more diverse and complicated phenomenon.” Her 1968 article, “The Tenacity of Tradition,” further broke ground by focusing on Qiu Jin and marking “a landmark in what one later scholar called ‘engendering the Chinese revolution.’” Her second monograph, Elite Activism and Political Transformation in China (Stanford 1986), showed how local literati power, first mobilized during the Taiping threat, evolved to render imperial rule “simply superfluous to the effective governance of the localities and the nation.” A co-edited volume, Chinese Local Elites and Patterns of Dominance (1990), extended her influence to a new generation of scholars. Although she never held a regular faculty position, Rankin became “arguably the most influential teacher in the field of Chinese social history” through her mentorship, editorial work with Late Imperial China, and her legendary “Rankin’s salon” in Georgetown, which served as “incubator for some of the most important new work on Chinese history.” (https://krieger.jhu.edu/east-asian/about/mary-rankin-reading-room/)

rows.value: Martina Deuchler, “a Swiss academic and author,” is a pioneering scholar in Korean studies whose work combines history and social anthropology to analyze Korea’s Confucian legacy. Educated at Leiden, Harvard, and Oxford, she earned her PhD with a dissertation titled The Opening of Korea, 1875–1884 (1967) under the mentorship of John K. Fairbank and Edwin O. Reischauer. Her major works include Confucian Gentlemen and Barbarian Envoys (1977), The Confucian Transformation of Korea (1992), and Under the Ancestors’ Eyes (2015). Her research has focused on “landed elites and their perception of the historic changes in East Asia at the end of the nineteenth century,” and she argued that “Neo-Confucianism, as a socio-political ideology, transformed the originally bilateral Korean society into a patrilineal one.” Deuchler conducted extensive fieldwork and archival research in Korea, gaining rare access to rural rituals, and played a vital role in institutionalizing Korean studies in Europe, co-founding the Association for Korean Studies in Europe (AKSE) in 1977. As professor at SOAS, she educated “future generations of Koreanists” and continued her research as a “Research Professor” and consultant well into retirement. rows.value: Mark Mancall, Stanford history professor emeritus, was a distinguished scholar of Central and Southeast Asian history, religions, languages, and cultures, authoring six major works including Russia and China: Their Diplomatic Relations to 1728 and China at the Center: Three Hundred Years of Foreign Policy. Jansen was an American historian and Emeritus Professor of Japanese History at Princeton University whose research focused on Japanese history and Japan’s interactions with China. He completed his PhD at Harvard in 1950 under Edwin O. Reischauer and John K. Fairbank, with his dissertation on Japan-China relations published as The Japanese and Sun Yat Sen (1954). His scholarship explored Japan’s modernization, political transitions, and international relations, with an intellectual trajectory marked by a commitment to understanding Japan’s transformation in a broader East Asian context. He was recognized as “the first foreigner to be honored with the Distinguished Cultural Merit Award” by Japan in 1999 and served as president of the Association for Asian Studies in 1976. His work was praised for combining rigorous historical analysis with cross-cultural insight, evident in statements like his study of the “interactions of the two countries” (Japan and China) and his role in illuminating “Two Centuries of Change” in Japan’s global position. rows.value: Marilyn B. Young was a historian of the United States and warfare, whose research spanned U.S.–China relations, the Vietnam War, empire, and American military interventions. Her intellectual trajectory began with The Rhetoric of Empire: American China Policy, 1895–1901 (1968), where she argued that U.S. policy in Asia “went beyond economic motives” and reflected a desire for world power presence, demonstrating her “great capacity to weave together international relations with domestic politics and culture.” She coauthored Transforming Russia and China: Revolutionary Struggle in the Twentieth Century (1982), critiquing American misunderstandings of revolution and social change. Her landmark work, The Vietnam Wars, 1945–1990 (1991), was “the first book to examine the war from the Vietnamese and American perspectives together,” emphasizing the plural “wars” to show the complexity and persistence of conflict. Throughout her career, she stressed that “war continues to be a primary instrument of American foreign policy,” critiquing the normalization of warfare in U.S. history. She was also a committed collaborator and activist, coediting collections such as Bombing Civilians: A Twentieth-Century History and participating in organizations like the Committee of Concerned Asian Scholars and Historians Against War. As she reflected in her 2011 presidential address to the Society for Historians of American Foreign Relations, “the shadow of war… seems not to be a shadow but entirely substantial: the substance of American history,” making her lifelong mission “to make war visible, vivid, an inescapable part of the country’s self-consciousness.” (https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/marilyn-b-young-1937-2017-may-2017/)

rows.value: Lloyd E. Eastman was a leading American scholar of Chinese history, specializing in the Republican period, whose intellectual trajectory moved from late Qing history—as seen in his first book Throne and Mandarins: China’s Search for a Policy During the Sino-French Controversy, 1880–1885 (1967)—to pioneering studies of twentieth-century China, exemplified by The Abortive Revolution: China under Nationalist Rule, 1927–1937 (1974) and Seeds of Destruction: Nationalist China in War and Revolution, 1937–1949 (1984). He posed “difficult, often politically charged questions” and argued provocatively that “the Kuomintang, after seizing power in 1927–1928, quickly lost revolutionary momentum and became a military dictatorship primarily concerned with maintaining itself in power,” setting a new standard for scholarship on the Nationalist regime despite limited access to sources. His intellectual rigor extended to social and economic history, as reflected in Family, Fields, and Ancestors: Constancy and Change in the Society and Economy of China, 1550–1949 (1988). Eastman was preparing a major study on Chiang Kai-shek, though illness prevented its completion; he edited Chiang Kai-shek’s Secret Past: The Memoir of His Second Wife, underscoring his bibliographical command and scholarly connections. Renowned for high scholarly standards and generosity, Eastman supported students and colleagues, helped organize the journal Republican China, and was esteemed both in the U.S. and among Chinese scholars in Taiwan and the PRC for balancing “bluntness and tact” in his scholarship and relationships. His career embodied “intellectual ambition, courage, and sanity,” and he remained a model teacher and mentor until his death in 1993. (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/FF8F7ED42184EC8DBB269964D0C9DF81/S0021911800036925a.pdf/lloyd-e-eastman-19291993.pdf)

rows.value: Liu Kwang-ching was a Chinese-born American historian specializing in late-Qing history, renowned for his “astute bibliographical work” and co-editing volumes of the Cambridge History of China; he taught at the University of California-Davis from 1963 until retirement in 1993. According to Wikipedia, Liu’s first major publication was Modern China: A Bibliographic Guide to Chinese Works, 1898-1937 (1950), co-edited with John Fairbank, praised for its detailed annotations and as “much more than a listing of titles” with “information as well as inspiration.” His intellectual trajectory included studying modern Chinese history at Harvard under Fairbank, earning his Ph.D. in 1956, working at the UN Secretariat, and then transitioning to academia with positions at Cambridge, Yale, and finally UC Davis. His scholarship is characterized by detailed bibliographical surveys and in-depth studies on political reform and orthodoxy in late imperial China, exemplified by edited volumes such as Orthodoxy in Late Imperial China (1990), where he explained the concept of 礼教 (lijiao) or “doctrine of propriety-and-ritual” as “orthodox” tradition, and Heterodoxy in Late Imperial China (2004). Liu was recognized for his “genius for bibliography” and his approach to “imagining what historians could do with available materials,” influencing both Sinology and historiography of China’s late imperial period. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Kwang-ching)

rows.value: Joseph Richmond Levenson, Sather Professor of History at UC Berkeley, was a pioneering intellectual historian of modern China whose work explored the profound dilemmas faced by individuals and societies amid cultural and historical transformation. Born in 1920 and educated at Harvard, Levenson shifted from European to Chinese history after World War II, reflecting his belief that "the questions which confront China are more and more becoming the same questions which confront us...which in a cosmopolitan world we all share." His dissertation and first major book, Liang Ch'i-ch'ao and the Mind of Modern China, examined how Liang struggled to reconcile "his intellectual alienation with his emotional bonds to Confucianism," illustrating how "history and value were torn apart in many Chinese minds" during times of upheaval. Levenson's scholarship is marked by a commitment to historical relativism and dialectics, rejecting simple narratives in favor of exploring “the problem of intellectual continuity” and the tensions between individuals, institutions, and cultural traditions, as elaborated in his trilogy Confucian China and its Modern Fate. Despite facing controversy—his relativism was sometimes misunderstood as a failure to engage politically—Levenson insisted that historians must "take one's own day seriously, retaining the moral need to declare oneself and stand somewhere." His Jewish identity deeply informed his work, framing his inquiry into how people live "choosing life itself" amid competing historical legacies. Levenson’s reflective approach linked Chinese intellectual history with universal human concerns about "ties that bind a world," and his legacy endures as a profound model of how to study culture, history, and identity with rigor, empathy, and a global vision. (https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1979/4/6/joseph-r-levenson-a-retrospective-pithis/)

rows.value: John Schrecker, Professor Emeritus of History at Brandeis University, has concentrated his scholarship on "Sino-Western relations in the 19th and 20th centuries" and "modern China’s relationship to its past." He is currently completing a biography of Anson Burlingame, “the anti-slavery politician who became Lincoln’s ambassador to China and China’s first ambassador to the United States,” highlighting his long-standing engagement with cross-cultural diplomacy and historical biography. Schrecker’s intellectual trajectory moves from focused case studies of imperialism toward broader syntheses of China’s modern transformation and its global entanglements. rows.value: John Israel is a historian of modern China whose intellectual trajectory was shaped by early studies at Harvard and deep field experience in Taiwan and mainland China, especially Yunnan. His research field centers on wartime Chinese intellectual life and U.S.–China academic exchange. After studying Chinese history under John King Fairbank and spending formative years in Taiwan (1959–1962), Israel first visited the PRC in 1978 and settled in Kunming in 1980 as “the first American exchange professor since 1949 to visit the province of Yunnan.” There he began his landmark project on The Southwest Associated University (Xinan Lianda), culminating in his major work Lianda: A Chinese University in War and Revolution (1998). He emphasized that “without the experience of living in Kunming, it would have been difficult to write” the book, which later “sold some 20,000 copies” in China and made him “a minor celebrity.” Rooted in microhistory, his scholarship tells stories that convey a “sense of the past to readers in the present.” Retired from teaching at the University of Virginia in 2003, he continues to live part-time in Kunming and is working on a new project about the “55 Educated Youth” (五十五知青), sent-down youths during the Cultural Revolution. rows.value: John E. Wills, Jr., a foundational scholar of Chinese and global history, began his career at USC in 1965 and continued contributing actively even after his 2004 retirement. His research, rooted in inter-cultural encounters, began with Pepper, Guns, and Parleys: The Dutch East India Company and China, 1662–1681 (1974), which “brought imperial and company concerns and the lives and tactics of traders to light.” Wills focused on “the problems of inter-cultural communication,” and his scholarship extended to major works like Embassies and Illusions (1984), the co-edited volume From Ming to Ch’ing (1979), and the widely acclaimed Mountain of Fame: Portraits in Chinese History (1995), which he called “a book about Chinese memory.” His global historical perspective culminated in 1688: A Global History (2001), described as “a Los Angeles Times bestseller” and “short-listed for a British PEN prize.” A polyglot and rigorous archival researcher, he drew on Dutch, Portuguese, Spanish, and Chinese sources across Asia and Europe. As noted by R. Bin Wong, Wills “pioneered the integration of Chinese history into broader regional and global historical scholarship.” Throughout his career, Wills was a devoted mentor and civic participant, establishing a research fellowship fund for graduate students and championing cross-cultural education, embodying, in the words of USC President C.L. rows.value: James C. Thomson Jr. was an American historian and journalist specializing in American-East Asian relations, particularly focusing on U.S. reform efforts in Nationalist China. His doctoral dissertation, published as While China Faced West: American Reformers in Nationalist China, 1928-1937 (1969), "describes the efforts of American oriented reformers to provide China with effective political and social change," notably the Rural Reconstruction Movement, blending “his own deep and personal interest” with critical analysis of the political contradictions involved. He supported John Fairbank's Committee on American-East Asian Relations and co-edited American-East Asian Relations: A Survey (1972), a foundational volume assessing the state of the field. Thomson also engaged in political work, serving as an advisor in the Kennedy administration and as a National Security Council China specialist before resigning in protest of the Vietnam War. His article "How Could Vietnam Happen?" (1968) critiques U.S. bureaucratic politics and policy failures. He later taught at Harvard and Boston University, contributing both academic and journalistic work. Thomson’s intellectual trajectory moved from detailed historical study of Sino-American reformers to broader reflections on U.S. foreign policy and East Asian relations, exemplified by his engagement with cultural figures such as Pearl S. Buck, whom he described as “the most influential writer on China since Marco Polo.” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_C._Thomson_Jr.)

Rawski, Distinguished University Professor Emerita of History, is a leading historian of late imperial China whose work spans Chinese economic history, social institutions, historiography, and the Qing dynasty's borderlands. Her early research focused on the rural economy, as seen in Agricultural Change and the Peasant Economy of South China (1972), and literacy, in Education and Popular Literacy in Ch’ing China (1979). She co-edited landmark volumes on popular culture, death rituals, and ritual music in China, including Popular Culture in Late Imperial China (1985) and Death Ritual in Late Imperial and Modern China (1988). Her most influential monograph, The Last Emperors: A Social History of Qing Imperial Institutions (1998), reinterprets the Qing court as "a vital institution of governance and cultural representation" rather than a decadent relic. In Early Modern China and Northeast Asia (2015), she challenges Sinocentric narratives by emphasizing the Qing Empire’s "multiethnic character and cross-border interactions." Her intellectual trajectory reflects a shift from economic and literacy studies to a broader cultural, institutional, and transregional analysis of Qing China. (https://www.history.pitt.edu/people/evelyn-rawski)
The research geography is late imperial China, South China, and Qing China.

rows.value: Eugene Powers Boardman was "a pioneer in East Asian history at the University of Wisconsin," with a scholarly focus on 19th-century Chinese religious movements and U.S.-China relations. His major work, Christian Influence upon the Ideology of the Taiping Rebellion, 1851–1854 (1952), examined the role of Christian ideas in the Taiping uprising. Boardman’s intellectual path included early teaching at the American University in Beirut (1932–35), wartime service as "a Japanese language officer in the United States Marine Corps," and academic positions at Wisconsin, where he joined the faculty in 1946 and became professor in 1961. He held a Fulbright at the University of Hong Kong (1951) and was a senior research fellow at Columbia’s East Asian Institute (1956–57). He also worked in Washington, D.C., as "a representative of the Society of Friends' Committee on National Legislation (1965–66)," advocating for a new China policy. Dreyer (1940–2007) was “an American historian known for his work and expertise on the history of China's Ming dynasty.” After earning his B.A. and Ph.D. in history from Harvard University—where his dissertation, The Emergence of Chu Yuan-chang, 1360–65, was advised by John Fairbank and Lien-sheng Yang—Dreyer spent most of his academic career at the University of Miami (1970–2007). His research focused on the “formative years” of the Ming state and its “military and naval history,” contributing, among other works, the chapter “Military Origins of Ming China” to The Cambridge History of China (vol. 7, part 1). He became a “leading global authority on the Battle of Lake Poyang and the expeditions of Zheng He,” underscoring his emphasis on the strategic and maritime dimensions of early Ming rule. Dreyer’s intellectual trajectory reflects a deep engagement with the military foundations of imperial authority and China's role in early global maritime history. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_L._Dreyer)

rows.value: Edward Friedman, Professor Emeritus of Political Science at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, specializes in "China, Democratization, Globalization, Human Rights, Political Economy, Postcommunism, [and] Revolution." His scholarship centers on Chinese domestic politics and international relations, particularly the tensions between authoritarianism and democratization. According to his biography, he “continues to teach and do research about Chinese foreign policy.” Among his major works are Chinese Village, Socialist State (1991), The Politics of Democratization: Generalizing the East Asian Experience (1994), and National Identity and Democratic Prospects in Socialist China (1995), reflecting his long-term focus on political transformation in China. He later authored What if China doesn’t democratize? Implications for war and peace (2001) and China’s Rise, Taiwan’s Dilemmas and International Peace (2005), exploring the geopolitical consequences of authoritarian persistence. In 2012, he also served as chief editor and organizer for the English translation of Yang Jisheng’s Tombstone, a searing study of “the worst famine in human history.” Friedman’s intellectual trajectory has consistently combined empirical research on rural China with broader theoretical concerns about democracy, identity, and peace in the post-communist world. (https://polisci.wisc.edu/staff/edward-friedman/)
The research geography is China and East Asia.

rows.value: Dr. Sarasin Viraphol, currently Executive Vice President of the Charoen Pokphand Group in Thailand, is a distinguished scholar and diplomat whose intellectual trajectory bridges academia, diplomacy, and business. Educated at Harvard University with an M.A. in Area Studies/East Asia and a Ph.D. in History and East Asian Languages, he began as a lecturer and assistant professor at Chulalongkorn University before transitioning to a diplomatic career in Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where he rose to the roles of Deputy Permanent Secretary and Ambassador to the Philippines. His major academic work includes Tribute and Profit: Sino-Siamese Trade, 1652–1853 (Harvard, 1977), which explores "the mechanisms and transformations of tributary trade and commercial profit between Siam and China." He has also written widely on Thai foreign policy, regional security, China’s rise, and ASEAN diplomacy, with titles such as Directions in Thai Foreign Policy (1976), The Thai Perception of China and Japan (1975), and The Soviet Threat: Development of the Thai Perception (1985). A recurrent theme in his work is the intersection of national security, economic policy, and historical consciousness, reflecting what he calls “Thai perceptions of external threat and opportunity,” as well as his pragmatic focus on “developing stronger business networks between ASEAN and China.” (https://www.turek-consulting.de/triangle/bios/viraphol.html; Google Scholar)
The research geography includes Thailand (Siam), China, and East Asia.

rows.value: David Tod Roy was a renowned American sinologist and scholar of Chinese literature who served as Professor of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago from 1967 to 1999, best known for his monumental five-volume English translation of Jin Ping Mei (The Plum in the Golden Vase)—“the first to render the whole novel into English.” Roy began this project in 1982 and completed it in 2012, describing it as a “life’s work of enviable concreteness: 3,493 pages, five volumes, and 13.5 pounds.” He undertook a painstaking effort to identify and annotate the text’s vast intertextual references, compiling over “10,000 three-by-five file cards” indexing allusions from earlier Chinese works. Reviewer Jonathan Spence praised Roy’s “splendid energy” and “precision, thoroughness, and passion for detail,” while Perry Link noted Roy's dedication to “translate everything—even puns.” Earlier in his career, Roy published Kuo Mo-Jo: The Early Years (1971), based on his doctoral thesis on the modern Chinese literary figure Guo Moruo, and co-edited Ancient China: Studies in Early Civilization (1978). Though drawn to Jin Ping Mei in his youth for its reputation as “pornographic,” Roy ultimately discovered “there was much more to it than that,” and he devoted three decades to revealing its literary richness to the English-speaking world. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tod_Roy)

rows.value: David Shepherd Nivison was a prominent American sinologist whose research spanned late imperial and ancient Chinese history, philology, and philosophy, with a long academic career at Stanford University. He is particularly noted for "his use of archaeoastronomy to accurately determine the date of the founding of the Zhou dynasty as 1045 BC instead of the traditional date of 1122 BC," later suggesting 1040 BC as more precise, and challenging official Chinese chronology projects. His intellectual trajectory involved rigorous training in both Chinese studies and analytic philosophy, having audited Willard Van Orman Quine’s Philosophy of Language course and applied analytic philosophical methods to Chinese thought. Nivison's major works include his award-winning doctoral dissertation on Qing philosopher Zhang Xuecheng, published as The Life and Thought of Chang Hsüeh-ch'eng, 1738-1801 (1966), and The Ways of Confucianism: Investigations in Chinese Philosophy (1996), reflecting his deep engagement with Confucian philosophy. He also edited Confucianism in Action (1959) and authored The Riddle of the Bamboo Annals (2009). Nivison’s scholarship was characterized by blending traditional sinological expertise with analytic clarity, notably evident in his efforts to reinterpret Chinese philosophical and historical traditions through modern methodologies. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Shepherd_Nivison)
The research geography is ancient and late imperial China.

rows.value: Benjamin I. Schwartz was an American political scientist and sinologist who “wrote on a wide range of topics in Chinese politics and intellectual history” and spent his entire career teaching at Harvard University, where he held the Leroy B. Williams Chair in History and Government from 1975 until his retirement in 1987. His early work, such as Chinese Communism and the Rise of Mao (1951), investigated Chinese communism’s “ideas, intentions, and ambitions” focusing on its “doctrinal frame of reference and internal political relations,” emphasizing that the leaders “would not automatically express the needs and aspirations of the masses.” Schwartz’s intellectual trajectory moved toward exploring the interaction between tradition, modernity, and identity, as in In Search of Wealth and Power: Yen Fu and the West (1964), where he analyzed how Yan Fu’s translations reflected Western influences that “subverted individual values.” Later, he produced influential collections like Communism and China: Ideology in Flux (1968), and his major work The World of Thought in Ancient China (1985) engaged deeply with Chinese intellectual traditions, earning extensive academic attention. He also edited Reflections on the May Fourth Movement (1972) and published China and Other Matters (1996), continuing to explore Chinese political thought and culture. Throughout, Schwartz combined political analysis with intellectual history, contributing significantly to understanding Chinese modernity and tradition, as well as the ideological complexities of Chinese communism. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_I._Schwartz)

rows.value: Arthur F. Wright was an American historian and sinologist specializing in Chinese social and intellectual history of the pre-modern period. He held academic positions at Stanford University and Yale University, becoming the Charles Seymour Professor of History at Yale in 1961. Wright believed that the scholar "should occasionally stand back and contemplate the whole continuum of time and of problems which give meaning to his specialized studies." His major works include Studies in Chinese Thought (1953), Buddhism in Chinese History (1957), Confucian Personalities (1962, co-edited with Denis Twitchett), Confucianism and Chinese Civilization (1964), and Perspectives on the Tʻang (1973), among others. His scholarship is characterized by a focus on the intellectual traditions of China, particularly Buddhism and Confucianism, contributing to a broad understanding of Chinese civilization. According to WorldCat, his writings encompass roughly 70+ works in over 200 publications across 6 languages, with 8,800+ library holdings, underscoring his intellectual impact in the field of sinology. He has also played a significant public role as “chair of the steering committee of the Center for the Study of Human Rights,” former board chair of Human Rights in China, and advisory board member at Human Rights Watch Asia. rows.value: Alexander Woodside, Professor Emeritus at the University of British Columbia, is a renowned historian specializing in Vietnamese and Chinese history, particularly state formation, ideology, education, and reform in both societies. His work frequently compares China and Vietnam, especially in the context of "intellectuals and the state" and their role in modern reform processes. In articles such as “Exalting the Latecomer State: Intellectuals and the State during the Chinese and Vietnamese Reforms” (1998), Woodside explores how these societies adapted to modernization by "reconceptualizing the state’s moral and political role." His early work, including “The Development of Social Organizations in Vietnamese Cities in the Late Colonial Period” (1971) and “Decolonization and Agricultural Reform in Northern Vietnam” (1970), focuses on colonial legacies and rural change. Over decades, his intellectual trajectory has been marked by efforts to "reconcile the Chinese and Western theory worlds" (1998) and to critique modernization narratives through deeply comparative and cross-cultural historical methods. Through his prolific reviews and scholarship, Woodside has helped reframe understandings of education, nationalism, and elite consciousness across East and Southeast Asia. (https://history.ubc.ca/profile/alexander-woodside/)

rows.value: Albert Feuerwerker was a historian of modern China specializing in economic history and a foundational figure in Chinese studies, notably serving as the first director of the University of Michigan’s Center for Chinese Studies (1961–1967, 1972–1983) and as president of the Association for Asian Studies (1991–1992). His doctoral dissertation was published as China’s Early Industrialization; Sheng Hsuan-huai (1844–1916) and Mandarin Enterprise (Harvard, 1958), which “explored the difficulties of a Confucian government in taking on the tasks of modernization.” He extended this theme in works like “Handicraft and Manufactured Cotton Textiles in China, 1871–1910” (1970), arguing, along with contemporaries like Joseph Levenson and Mary C. Wright, that “traditional Chinese values were a barrier to modernity and would have to be dismantled before China could make progress.” Feuerwerker also critically engaged with Marxist historiography of China in essays such as “China’s History in Marxian Dress” and co-edited History in Communist China (1968), a volume analyzing PRC historiography. His intellectual trajectory encompassed pioneering economic history research, institutional leadership in area studies, and editorial work, including contributions to The Cambridge History of China and volumes such as Approaches to Modern Chinese History (1967). He is recognized for shaping the field of Chinese studies during the Cold War and for his critical engagement with the ideological frameworks shaping Chinese historiography. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Feuerwerker)

rows.value: Akira Iriye is an American historian specializing in diplomatic, international, and transnational history, with a focus on U.S., China, and Japan relations before and during the Pacific War. Educated at Haverford College and Harvard University, where he studied under John K. Fairbank and Ernest R. May, Iriye’s scholarship is marked by “multi-archival and multi-lingual research.” His first major work, After Imperialism: The Search for a New Order in the Far East, 1921–1931 (1965), argued that the collapse of the "diplomacy of imperialism" after the Treaty of Versailles left “a vacuum in the East Asian international system.” He further developed this theme in Pacific Estrangement: Japanese and American Expansion, 1897–1911 (1972) and explored cultural parallels in Power and Culture: The Japanese-American War, 1941–1945 (1981), which was a Pulitzer Prize finalist. Iriye expanded traditional diplomatic history by incorporating cultural perspectives and international relations, exemplified in works such as Across the Pacific: An Inner History of American-East Asian Relations (1965) and his involvement in founding the Journal of American-East Asian Relations. His intellectual trajectory moved toward a broader global and transnational history, as reflected in his 1988 American Historical Association presidential address, "The Internationalization of History," where he called for historians to seek “historical themes and conceptions that are meaningful across national boundaries,” and in later works like Cultural Internationalism and World Order (1997) and Global Community (2002), which focus on NGOs and global consciousness rather than traditional diplomacy. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_Iriye)
